relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is SPPL2a deficiency and mycobacterial disease, but it incidentally reports two Moroccan sisters from a consanguineous family with hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous AP4E1 nonsense variant, the gene/disorder of this entry.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2018) reported that monozygotic twin sisters (P1 and P2), born in 2009 to first-cousin Moroccan parents and studied primarily for Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, also displayed hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous p.R1105X mutation of the AP4E1 gene.
quotes: In addition to MSMD, the patients displayed hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous p.R1105X mutation of the AP4E1 gene.
Two of the patients studied (P1 and P2) are twins born in 2009 to first-cousin Moroccan parents.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2018) described the two affected eight-year-old monozygotic twin sisters (P1 and P2) from a consanguineous Moroccan kindred, who in addition to their hereditary spastic paraplegia had BCG disease: they presented at nine months of age with unilaterally enlarged inflammatory axillary lymph nodes after BCG vaccination at birth, with biopsy confirming acid-fast bacilli; neonatal asphyxiation had been noted during delivery.
quotes: a family from Morocco including two affected eight-year-old monozygotic twin sisters (P1 and P2, Kindred A, Fig. 1a)

They were vaccinated with BCG at birth and presented with unilaterally enlarged and inflammatory axillary lymph nodes at nine months of age. The enlarged lymph nodes were surgically removed. Biopsy confirmed the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB), consistent with mycobacterial infection.
No complications had been observed during the pregnancy, but neonatal asphyxiation was noted during the delivery.

phenotypes.text: normal counts of neutrophils, monocytes, B, T and NK cells

relevance_reason: Reports Moroccan twins with SPG51 caused by a novel homozygous AP4E1 nonsense mutation, with clinical, molecular and functional data.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) reported identical female twins born to first-cousin Moroccan parents who had infancy-onset complex hereditary spastic paraplegia. At age 3 years they had marked developmental delay, microcephaly, inability to walk, absent speech, stereotypic laughter, drooling, muscular hypotonia, short stature and low body weight, and spastic paraplegia of the lower extremities. They did not have seizures. They had a prominent bulbous nose, wide mouth and coarse features. CT showed atrophy of the inferior vermis with cortical atrophy, and EEG showed diffuse slow waves.
quotes: The two patients (P1 and P2) are identical twins born to first-cousin Moroccan parents (Figure 1A).

When examined at the age of three years, the twins displayed marked developmental retardation, including microcephaly, an inability to walk unaided, abnormal speech and abnormal circadian development. They kept smiling or laughing for no obvious reason.

Both patients presented discreet but remarkable facial gestalt with a prominent, bulbous nose, a wide mouth and coarse features. Neurological examination revealed spastic paraplegia of the lower extremities.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) reported that both twins developed unilateral enlarged, inflamed axillary lymph nodes at 9 months of age after BCG vaccination. Biopsy showed acid-fast bacilli. Immune cell counts, immunoglobulins and complement were normal, and the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis and oxidative burst were normal. The authors proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease.
quotes: In addition to neurologic problems, both patients presented unilaterally enlarged and inflammatory axillary lymph nodes at nine months of age.
Biopsy confirmed the presence of acid-fast bacilli, consistent with mycobacterial infection.
We thus propose that the AP4E1 mutation is the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease in our patients.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) used whole-exome sequencing in twins with SPG51 born to consanguineous Moroccan parents and identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the AP4E1 gene (p.R1105X). Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation. It segregated with the disorder: both parents were heterozygous and a healthy sib was wildtype. The mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or in 69 Moroccan controls.
quotes: We found only one homozygous nonsense mutation in AP4E1 (Figure 1B, Table 2), resulting in the replacement of an arginine residue in position 1105 with a premature stop codon (p.R1105X).
both P1 and P2 carried the same homozygous mutation, whereas the parents were heterozygous and a healthy sibling was wild-type at this locus (Figure 1A).

This variant was not found in the sequences of 1,050 healthy controls from 51 ethnic groups from the Centre d'Étude du Polymorphisme Humain (CEPH) panel [35], [36] or in an additional 69 Moroccan controls.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) found that the p.R1105X mutation did not affect AP4E1 mRNA levels or splicing in patient EBV-B cells. However, AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and AP-4-mu and AP-4-beta levels were also lower. Assembled AP-4 complex was more than 95% lower in patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells, and the AP-4 binding partner tepsin was undetectable in patient fibroblasts. The authors suggested that the C-terminal part of AP-4-epsilon is important for the integrity of the AP-4 complex.
quotes: The levels of mRNA for AP4E1, AP4B1, AP4M1 and AP4S1 did not differ significantly between cells from P1 and control cells (expressed relative to GUS; Figure 2A).

AP-4ε was barely detectable in EBV-B cells from P1, but was clearly present in control cells (Figure 2C). In addition, the loss of AP-4ε resulted in a concomitant decrease in the levels of both the AP-4 μ and AP-4β proteins in the patient’s cells.
IMAGE J quantification indicated that AP-4 assembly levels were more than 95% lower than those of healthy controls

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) noted that p.R1105X lies close to the normal termination codon and does not trigger nonsense-mediated decay. They speculated that the resulting C-terminally truncated protein might have dominant-negative or gain-of-function activity, which could explain why mycobacterial disease occurred in these patients but not in other AP-4-deficient patients, most of whom carry probable null mutations.
quotes: In our case, the nonsense mutation p.R1105X, which is located close to the normal translation termination codon (p.X1137), does not generate a transcript subject to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) [48].
This escape from NMD may lead to the production of a C-terminally truncated protein, which may display a dominant-negative activity or a deleterious gain of function.

findings.statement: Kong et al. (2013) noted that 27 patients from 9 kindreds with mutations in AP-4 subunit genes (AP4E1, AP4B1, AP4S1 and AP4M1) share a uniform phenotype of complex HSP: severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, progressive spastic paraplegia, growth retardation and stereotypic laughter. They called this phenotype 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome.'
quotes: In total, 27 patients from nine kindreds, including nine with AP4E1 mutations, nine with AP4B1 mutations, six with AP4S1 mutations, and three with AP4M1 mutations [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], have a uniform clinical phenotype of type I complex HSP, characterized by severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, progressive spastic paraplegia, growth retardation and a stereotypical laugh.

relevance_reason: Only the abstract is available. It describes a large homozygosity mapping and next-generation sequencing study of consanguineous families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, but it does not name SPG51, its gene, or any specific family or variant relevant to this entry.

findings.statement: Najmabadi et al. (2011) performed homozygosity mapping, exon enrichment, and next-generation sequencing in 136 consanguineous families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability from Iran and elsewhere. They found additional mutations in 23 genes previously implicated in intellectual disability or related neurologic disorders, and single, probably disease-causing variants in 50 novel candidate genes.
quotes: we have now performed homozygosity mapping, exon enrichment and next-generation sequencing in 136 consanguineous families with autosomal-recessive intellectual disability from Iran and elsewhere

has revealed additional mutations in 23 genes previously implicated in intellectual disability or related neurological disorders, as well as single, probably disease-causing variants in 50 novel candidate genes

relevance_reason: Reports a homozygous-presumed splice mutation in AP4E1 in a consanguineous family with severe intellectual disability and progressive spastic paraplegia, along with AP4B1 and AP4S1 mutations that define the AP4-deficiency syndrome.

findings.statement: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) reported 8 affected individuals from 3 consanguineous families with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, shy character, stereotypic laughter, muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia, microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation. The authors concluded that these findings demonstrated a clinically recognizable syndrome due to deficiency of the AP4 complex.
quotes: we report on eight affected individuals who were from three consanguineous families and presented with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, shy character, stereotypic laughter, muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia, microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation
demonstrate the existence of a clinically recognizable syndrome due to deficiency of the AP4 complex

phenotypes.text: decreased muscle mass of lower limbs

findings.statement: In affected members of a consanguineous family with severe intellectual disability and progressive spastic paraplegia, Abou Jamra et al. (2011) identified a splice mutation in the AP4E1 gene (c.542+1_542+4delGTAA, NM_007347.3), resulting in skipping of sequence (r.421_542del) and a frameshift (p.Glu181GlyfsTer20). The mutation was identified using a combination of autozygosity mapping and either Sanger sequencing of candidate genes or next-generation exome sequencing.
quotes: Using a combination of autozygosity mapping and either Sanger sequencing of candidate genes or next-generation exome sequencing, we identified one mutation in each of three genes encoding adaptor protein complex 4 (AP4) subunits
a splice mutation in AP4E1 (NM_007347.3: c.542+1_542+4delGTAA, r.421_542del, p.Glu181Glyfs(∗)20)

findings.statement: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) found that the same AP4-deficiency phenotype was caused by mutations in genes encoding other AP4 subunits in the 2 other consanguineous families: a nonsense mutation in AP4S1 (c.124C>T, p.Arg42Ter) and a frameshift mutation in AP4B1 (c.487_488insTAT, p.Glu163_Ser739delinsVal). They noted that mutations in AP4M1 and AP4E1 had recently been found to cause cerebral palsy associated with severe intellectual disability, supporting a crucial role of AP4-mediated trafficking in brain development and function.
quotes: a nonsense mutation in AP4S1 (NM_007077.3: c.124C>T, p.Arg42(∗)), a frameshift mutation in AP4B1 (NM_006594.2: c.487_488insTAT, p.Glu163_Ser739delinsVal)
Interestingly, two mutations affecting AP4M1 and AP4E1 have recently been found to cause cerebral palsy associated with severe intellectual disability.
these results support the hypothesis that AP4-complex-mediated trafficking plays a crucial role in brain development and functioning

relevance_reason: This is the first report of AP4E1 deficiency causing autosomal recessive spastic tetraplegic cerebral palsy (SPG51): a consanguineous family carrying a homozygous 15q21.2 deletion.

findings.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) described 2 sibs, a female (IV-4) examined at age 23 and a male (IV-5) examined at age 22, from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family. Both had autosomal recessive spastic tetraplegic cerebral palsy with profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy and white matter loss. Both were born at term after uneventful pregnancies and had microcephaly and hypotonia from birth or soon after. The hypotonia progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia, hyperreflexia and Babinski signs. Both later had generalized tonic-clonic seizures, stereotypic laughter, drooling, absent normal speech and absent sphincter control, and both became wheelchair-bound.
quotes: We evaluated a Palestinian–Jordanian consanguineous family with two siblings affected by an idiopathic neurological condition described as cerebral palsy
At birth she presented with microcephaly and hypotonia that progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalised hypertonia by the first year of life.
On examination at 22 years, he had spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia and hyperreflexia, outbursts of stereotypic laughter, drooling, and jerky nystagmus.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with generalized onset

findings.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) reported that the affected female sib had dysmorphic features. These included bitemporal narrowing, a long narrow face with a prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, a long nose with a wide nasal ridge, a short philtrum with a full everted upper vermilion, prominent antehelices and facial hypotonia. Her brother's dysmorphic features were described as very similar. Her brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was most pronounced frontally and in the corpus callosum. Her EEG showed generalized theta slowing of the background. Her brother's CT scan showed ventriculomegaly with prominent cisterns. Eye and hearing evaluations were normal in both sibs.
quotes: Dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, long narrow face with prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, long nose with wide nasal ridge, short philtrum with everted full upper vermillion, prominent antehelix of the ears, and facial hypotonia.
A brain MRI revealed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was more pronounced in the frontal region and corpus callosum
A head CT scan showed moderate ventriculomegaly with slightly prominent cisterns.

findings.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) used chromosomal microarray analysis to identify a homozygous deletion on chromosome 15q21.2 in the 2 affected sibs. High-resolution array mapping defined the deletion as 192 kb (chr15:48,835,480-49,028,171, hg18). It removed the 5-prime ends of AP4E1 and SPPL2A, and FISH confirmed the result. FISH showed that the mother was a heterozygous carrier, and SNRPN methylation analysis showing biparental inheritance of chromosome 15 indicated that the father was also a carrier. The authors proposed that AP4E1 deficiency was the main cause of the phenotype, although they could not rule out a contribution from loss of SPPL2A.
quotes: used this array to define the size of the deleted region to 192 kb (chr15:48835480-49028171; hg18 genome assembly, figure 1B, C)

We identified a 139 kb (minimum) to 222 kb (maximum) homozygous deletion of chromosome 15q21.2 that includes the 5′ end of two genes: AP4E1 (adaptor related protein complex-4, epsilon-1) and SPPL2A (signal peptide peptidase-like-2A).
FISH analysis on the mother revealed that she is a heterozygous carrier of the deletion.

variants.as_reported: 192 kb homozygous deletion of chromosome 15q21.2 including 5' end of AP4E1 and SPPL2A

findings.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) found that both affected sibs carried a homozygous 192-kb deletion at chromosome 15q21.2, which they confirmed by metaphase FISH using the RP11-147B19 probe. The mother and the older sister carried the deletion heterozygously, and the younger sib was not deleted.
quotes: The probe within the deleted interval was RP11-147B19, and the control probe outside the region was D15Z1, corresponding to the centromeric region of chromosome 15 (figure 1D).
middle panel, heterozygous deletion identified in the mother and older sister (III-2, IV-3); bottom panel, homozygous deletion found in both probands (IV-4, IV-5).

findings.statement: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) compared their AP4E1-deleted family with a Moroccan family in which Verkerk et al. had reported a homozygous AP4M1 mutation. The two families shared infantile hypotonia that progressed to spastic tetraplegia, microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, stereotypic laughter, drooling, ventriculomegaly and white matter loss. Epilepsy was present in the AP4E1 patients but not in the AP4M1 patients. The authors proposed that disrupting any of the 4 AP-4 subunits abolishes the function of the complex and causes a distinct autosomal recessive 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome'.
quotes: They presented with infantile hypotonia that progressed to spastic tetraplegia, hypertonia and hyperreflexia by the first year of life, microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, stereotypic laughter, and drooling.
Therefore, we propose that disruption of any one of the four subunits of AP-4 abolishes its function and causes a distinct autosomal recessive disorder that we refer to as ‘AP-4 deficiency syndrome’.
